text:
The concept of relativity, specifically time dilation, can be understood by comparing time to a rubber band that stretches or shrinks based on how fast you are moving or how strong the gravity is around you.

Imagine time is like a rubber band. If you are standing still on solid ground (normal gravity, low speed), the rubber band is at its normal length. Now, imagine you get into a super-fast spaceship that moves close to the speed of light. For you inside the ship, the rubber band feels normal—you age and experience life at a regular pace. However, to someone watching you from Earth, your rubber band appears stretched out. Because it is stretched, the "ticks" of your clock (the marks on the rubber band) happen much less frequently from their perspective. This means that while you might feel like only a few hours have passed, years might have passed for the person on Earth. Similarly, if you were near a massive object like a black hole, the intense gravity would pull on the "rubber band" of time, stretching it even more and causing time to slow down significantly compared to someone far away from the black hole.
